objectives: Read the ingredient list from the heaviest item down.
Tell a use-by date from a best-before date and act on each one correctly.
Find the nutrition panel and say what a serving really is.
Recognise the allergen statements that are printed in bold.
Check a package for damage, tampering and temperature abuse.
Ask a shop assistant the right question about a date you do not trust.
Explain to someone else how to store the food you have just bought.

sections.body:
A food package is a legal document. Every word on it is there because a law requires it, and the layout is nearly the same in every country because the rules were written to make the label comparable.

The front of the package is advertising. It carries the name of the product, the picture, and the claim the maker wants you to buy on. Ignore it for now and turn the package over. The back carries five parts, and they are always in the same order.

First the **name of the food**, in the law of the country it was made in. Sometimes the legal name sounds different from the name on the front: a jar that says "spicy tomato sauce" on the front may legally be called "tomato concentrate with added chilli and sugar" on the back.

Second the **ingredient list**, in order of weight. The first ingredient is the heaviest thing in the pack, the last is the lightest. This is the single most useful fact on the label, and it is the one people never look at.

Third the **allergen statement**. In most countries the fourteen allergens that can cause a serious reaction are named in the list, sometimes in bold, sometimes in their own box: cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, peanuts, soya beans, milk, nuts, celery, mustard, sesame, sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg/kg, lupin, and molluscs.

Fourth the **nutrition panel**, giving the energy and the fat, the saturates, the carbohydrate, the sugars, the protein and the salt for a stated amount of the product.

Fifth the **date and the storage instruction**, usually on the lid or the base: a use-by date, a best-before date, and the temperature the product has to stay at.

Read them in that order and you know more about a product than most people ever will.
examples: Turn the packet over and read the ingredients first.
The legal name of the product is on the back, under the ingredients.
sections.heading: What is actually printed on the package

sections.body:
Ingredients are listed by weight before the cooking, not by how much of it there is in the finished product. Water counts as an ingredient, so a soup that is mostly water can put water first and still be mostly vegetables in the bowl.

This is where the list earns its keep. If sugar appears three times under three different names, the product is trying to hide how sweet it is. Look for the family: sugar, glucose, fructose, sucrose, maltose, honey, syrup, concentrated fruit juice, maltodextrin, and the syrups that hide in savoury food. Two or three of those in one list means the product is mostly sweet, whatever the front says.

The same trick works in the other direction. A product that says "no added sugar" may still contain more sugar than a cake, because the sugar came from the fruit concentrate rather than from the sugar tin. "No added sugar" is a statement about the recipe, not about the sugar in your mouth.

Salt hides under several names too: salt, sodium, monosodium glutamate, and the disodium forms used as raising agents. If you are trying to cut salt, read the ingredients for "sodium" and not only for the word "salt".

The order also tells you about texture. Something listed first as "wheat flour" and then far down as "sugar" is a bread-like product. Something where sugar comes before the flour is a cake, and it should be eaten as one.

Some ingredients carry a technical name the shopper is not expected to recognise: "ascorbic acid" is vitamin C, "niacin" is vitamin B3, and "tartaric acid" is what makes a wine bottle stable. You are not expected to know them, but you are allowed to look them up, and a shop that cannot tell you what an ingredient is has no business selling it to you.
examples: Sugar is listed first, so this is a sweet product.
Look for the sodium content, not just the salt.
sections.heading: The ingredient list is a weight, not a menu

sections.body:
The two dates are the most confused words on any package, and the confusion has a cost, because people throw away good food and keep bad food.

A **use-by date** is a safety date. After it, the product may make you ill. Raw meat, fish, dairy, cooked meals, and anything with a life of its own carry one. The manufacturer is telling you the point after which the product is no longer safe to eat, and the date is not negotiable. If a pack of chicken is past its use-by date, throw it away. There is no smell test and no cooking trick that makes it safe, because the risk is not always something you can smell.

A **best-before date** is about quality, not safety. After it, the product is still perfectly safe; it has simply gone down in taste, texture or colour. Biscuits go soft, crisps go stale, oils go rancid. A jar of coffee or a tin of beans past its best-before date is not going to hurt you.

Some countries use a third line: **eat within** for food that is perishable but where the date is advisory.

Then there is the frozen food that says "best before end of". That date is about the quality of the product once thawed, not about a safety limit at all.

The date format itself is a trap. In most of Europe the format is day-month-year, so 04/05 is the fourth of May. In the United States and Canada it is month-day-year, so the same 04/05 is the fourth of May in Chicago and 5 April in Berlin. If a date is close to the day you are reading it, check which order the country uses before you decide.

And a date means nothing without the conditions. A "use by 12 June" on a pack that says "keep refrigerated below 5 °C" is a promise that only holds if the cold chain was never broken. Buy from a shop where the fridge is cold and the ice cream is solid, not from one where it has begun to melt.
examples: This is a use-by date, so I cannot sell it past this point.
Best-before is about quality, not about safety.
This date is day-month-year, so it is the fifth of April.
sections.heading: Use-by and best-before: two dates, two different promises

sections.body: Throw away any food with a use-by date that has passed, any food that smells wrong, any food that has swollen or burst, and any tinned food that is dented along a seam or bulging at the end. Never taste food to find out whether it is safe. Wash your hands, and clean the fridge when you find something bad, because the neighbours of a bad pot are usually bad too.
sections.heading: When you throw food away

sections.body:
The nutrition panel gives the figures for a serving. The serving is whatever the manufacturer decided to call a serving, and it is often smaller than the portion people actually eat.

Read four things on the panel. The **energy**, in kilocalories and usually also in kilojoules, tells you how much work the food is going to cost you. The **saturates** tell you about the saturated fat, which is the part of the fat that matters most for the heart. The **sugars** include the ones that come in naturally, so a portion of dried fruit can carry a lot of sugar without anything added to it. The **salt**, in grams, is usually the one people want and rarely look at.

Check the serving size against what you would actually eat. A cereal box that claims 30 g a serving is not describing the bowl most people pour. A bottle of juice that says 250 ml a serving is describing one small glass out of the bottle in your hand.

The reference intake is the daily guide the numbers are measured against. It is roughly 2000 kilocalories a day for an adult, and it is a general figure, not a target: a person who cycles forty kilometres a day does not need the same as a person who sits at a desk, and a child needs less than an adult of the same weight.

Two claims on the front of the package are worth checking against the panel. "Low fat" usually means under 3 g of fat per 100 g, and a low-fat cake can be full of sugar. "No added sugar" says nothing about the sugar in the fruit. "Source of fibre" means at least 3 g per 100 g, which is a modest amount in absolute terms. Read the panel, not the claim.
examples: This serving is 30 grams, but I will eat twice that.
The label says low fat, so I checked the sugar as well.
sections.heading: The nutrition panel and the serving that is not the packet

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet on the shelf, and what each one actually obliges the maker to do.

**Per 100 g** is the standard measure that lets you compare two products fairly. **Per serving** is whatever the maker calls a serving, which is convenient for them and unhelpful for you. **Per portion** means the same thing, usually.

**kcal** is kilocalories: the energy in one gram of fat is nine kilocalories, in a gram of carbohydrate or protein it is four, and in a gram of alcohol it is seven. **kJ** is kilojoules, the same energy in the metric system. One kilocalorie is 4.18 kilojoules.

**Reference intake** is the daily average for an adult. **Daily value** is the American equivalent and is printed on a package sold in the United States.

**Whey, skimmed, semi-skimmed and whole** describe how much fat was taken out of the milk. **UHT** means ultra-high-temperature treated: heated briefly to make the milk keep without a fridge. **Pasteurised** means heated enough to kill most bacteria. **HACCP** on a fish or meat label is a statement about how the factory controlled contamination, not about the product being better.

**Trace** means the ingredient is present in an amount too small to be worth measuring, usually under 0.5 %. **May contain** means the same line is used in the factory, so the product may carry traces of it.

**Free from** is a claim about what is NOT in the product: no gluten, no added sugar, no dairy. It is only as good as the testing behind it.

**Best served within** and **once opened** are the storage instructions: the second one means the clock starts when you open the jar, not when it was made.
sections.heading: The words on a label, one by one

terms.example: This bar contains 250 kcal, which is about a tenth of a day's energy.
terms.gloss: A unit of energy in food. One gram of fat holds about 9 kcal, a gram of carbohydrate or protein about 4.

terms.example: The best-before date has passed, so the biscuits are only stale, not bad.
terms.gloss: The date after which the food is still safe to eat but has gone down in quality. A quality date, not a safety date.

terms.example: The use-by date was yesterday, so I threw the chicken away.
terms.gloss: The date after which the food may no longer be safe to eat. It is a safety date and it is not negotiable.

terms.example: One serving is 30 g, which is much less than the bowl I had.
terms.gloss: The amount of the product the nutrition figures are given for. It is the maker's choice, so it often does not match what you eat.

terms.example: The allergen box says it contains peanuts and soya.
terms.gloss: A substance in food that can cause a serious allergic reaction in some people. There are fourteen that have to be declared.

sections.body:
Pick the product up and turn it over once. Look at the date first, because a date that has passed makes everything else irrelevant. Then check the storage instruction and ask yourself whether this shop could keep that promise: a product that must stay below 5 °C has to come from a fridge that is actually cold.

Then look at the seal. A can should be flat at both ends; if one end is domed, do not buy it. A jar lid should be flat and firm, and it should not rattle when you turn it. A vacuum-sealed pack should be tight against the food with no liquid pooled in the corner. A carton that has leaked or swollen has been warm for too long.

Look at the pack itself for tears, punctures, and a corner chewed by a rodent. Check the date code on the base of the pack, not only the printed label on the front, because the printed label is the seller's promise and the stamped code is the factory's.

And check the weight against the price. The price per kilogram is the only comparison that means anything, and it is printed on the shelf ticket in most countries. Two packs of the same product at different prices are often the same weight at different sizes, and the shelf ticket is where that shows up.
examples: The lid is bulging, so I am putting it back.
The shelf ticket says 4.20 per kilogram, and the other one is 6.80.
sections.heading: What to check at the shelf, in thirty seconds
steps: Pick the pack up and turn it over.
Check that the storage instruction can be kept here.
Check the seal: flat, firm, tight.

sections.body: You can still read almost any food label without the language. The layout is the same everywhere: the ingredients are the long list, the allergens are the bold ones, the nutrition panel is the box with the little table, the date is the shortest line of numbers on the pack, and the storage instruction is the one with a temperature in it. Learn those five shapes once and you can shop in any country in the world.
sections.heading: A label in a language you do not read

sections.body:
Sometimes you need to ask. The assistant knows more about the stock than the label does: which batch it came from, how long it has been on the shelf, whether the fridge is working today.

Ask a closed question when you can, because it gets a straight answer. "Is this the use-by date or the best-before date?" is better than "Is this still good?". "Has this been out of the cold chain?" is better than "Is this safe?". "Do you have one from yesterday?" is better than "Is there another one?".

And if you are the one being asked, the honest answers are the ones that keep people safe. If the shop cannot keep the cold chain, say so on the ticket. If a product is withdrawn, take it off the shelf. Nobody is ever scolded for throwing away a bad pot of soup, and everybody is affected when it is not thrown away.
examples: Is that the use-by date or the best-before date?
Has this been in the fridge all day?
Does this need to go in a bag when I buy it?
sections.heading: Asking, and being asked

sections.body:
A date is a promise about the future, and the promise only holds if the storage rules were followed.

**Keep refrigerated below 5 °C** is the standard for anything fresh. Domestic fridges are usually colder than that at the back and warmer in the door, so keep milk, meat and opened jars away from the door and never in the vegetable drawer, which is the warmest place in the box.

**Keep frozen** means minus 18 °C or colder. A freezer that holds a bag of frozen peas is the test: if the peas are solid, the temperature is right.

**Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight** is the instruction for oil, flour, biscuits, tinned food and anything in glass. Heat and light are what spoil the fat and fade the colour.

**Once opened, keep refrigerated and use within three days** is the most common instruction in the world, and it is the one most often ignored. A jar of pesto, a pack of cooked rice and a tub of hummus all carry it. Write the date on the container when you open it; the date printed on the jar says nothing about the jar in your fridge.

**Do not refreeze after thawing** is not a quality warning but a safety one, for meat, fish and ready meals. If you have bought too much, freeze it before it thaws, not after.
examples: Once opened, keep it in the fridge and use it within three days.
I wrote the date on the tub when I opened it.
sections.heading: Storing it, so the date means something

terms.example: The cold chain was broken, so the date on the pack means nothing.
terms.gloss: The unbroken path a chilled product follows from the factory to your fridge. If the chain breaks, the use-by date stops meaning anything.

terms.example: You can freeze it now, but you cannot refreeze it once it has thawed.
terms.gloss: To put something that has thawed back into the freezer. For meat and fish this is a safety question, not a quality one.

item.summary: A food label tells you three things: what is inside, how much of it there is, and how long it is safe. After reading this you can read any label in any country, tell a use-by date from a best-before date, and decide at the shelf whether a product is worth buying.
item.title: Reading Food Labels and Expiration Dates
